answers.question: List of scenarios
answers.answer: Three scenarios were used: 1) Orderly (1.5°C), 2) Too Little Too Late (>2°C), and 3) Hot House (>3°C)
answers.evidence: "Three scenario narratives and four time horizons were developed to promote alignment of climate-related scenario analysis and risk disclosures across New Zealand's banking sector... Scenario dimensions: Orderly 1.5°C | Too Little Too Late >2°C | Hothouse >3°C"
answers.notes: The three scenarios are explicitly named and described in the document. They are aligned to IPCC SSP1-1.9, SSP2-4.5, and SSP5-8.5 respectively.

answers.question: Global temperature outcome by 2100
answers.answer: The document describes three scenarios with the following global temperature outcomes by 2100: Orderly scenario: 1.5°C; Too Little Too Late scenario: >2°C; Hot House scenario: >3°C.
answers.evidence: "Orderly 1.5⁰C | Too Little Too Late (>2⁰C) | Hot House (>3⁰C)"
answers.location_hint: Page 15, Table of Key scenario dimensions
answers.notes: The document uses three scenarios aligned to IPCC pathways: Orderly (1.5°C, SSP1-1.9), Too Little Too Late (>2°C, SSP2-4.5), and Hot House (>3°C, SSP5-8.5).

answers.question: Scenario provider
answers.answer: The scenario narratives were commissioned by the New Zealand Banking Association (NZBA) on behalf of its members, and developed by EY. The scenarios draw on international providers including NGFS (Network for Greening the Financial System), IEA (International Energy Agency), IPCC, NIWA, and the Climate Change Commission (CCC).
answers.evidence: "The work to compile the narratives was commissioned by the NZBA on behalf of its members, and developed by EY." and scenario dimensions include "NGFS Net Zero 2050 / IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (NZE) / NGFS Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC's) / IEA Announced Pledges (APS) / NGFS Current Policies / IEA Stated Policies (STEPS) / NIWA RCP2.6 / NIWA RCP4.5 / NIWA RCP8.5 / CCC 'Tailwinds' / CCC 'Headwinds' / CCC 'Current Policy Reference'"
answers.notes: The scenario narratives were developed by EY on behalf of NZBA members. The underlying scenario parameters come from multiple providers: NGFS, IEA, IPCC, NIWA, and the New Zealand Climate Change Commission (CCC).

answers.question: Pick-and-mix of SSPs and RCPs
answers.answer: Yes. The document uses a mix of SSPs and RCPs across different scenarios. For global climate & socio-economic parameters, it uses IPCC SSP1-1.9 (Orderly 1.5°C), IPCC SSP2-4.5 (Too Little Too Late >2°C), and IPCC SSP5-8.5 (Hothouse >3°C). For New Zealand-specific climate parameters, it uses NIWA RCP2.6 (Orderly), NIWA RCP4.5 (Too Little Too Late), and NIWA RCP8.5 (Hothouse). Physical risk modelling specifically uses RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, and RCP 8.5.
answers.evidence: "Global climate & socio-economic parameters: IPCC SSP1-1.9 | IPCC SSP2-4.5 | IPCC SSP5-8.5 ... New Zealand-specific climate parameters: NIWA RCP2.6 | NIWA RCP4.5 | NIWA RCP8.5" and "Scenario dimensions: RCP 2.6 | RCP 4.5 | RCP 8.5"
answers.location_hint: Table 1, p.13 (Strategy section) and Figure 21, p.34
answers.notes: The document uses SSPs for global parameters and RCPs for NZ-specific parameters, effectively mixing the two frameworks across different levels of analysis. Physical risk modelling uses RCPs only.

answers.question: Customised scenarios
answers.notes: The document does not describe any customised (bespoke) scenarios developed by CCB NZL. Instead, it uses the common set of scenario narratives developed by the New Zealand Banking Association (NZBA) on behalf of its members and developed by EY — three standard scenarios: Orderly (1.5°C), Too Little Too Late (>2°C), and Hot House (>3°C). No customised scenarios are mentioned.

answers.question: Co-produced climate scenarios
answers.answer: Yes. CCB NZL co-produced climate scenarios through the New Zealand Banking Association (NZBA). The work was commissioned by the NZBA on behalf of its members and developed by EY. Three scenario narratives were developed: Orderly (1.5°C, aligned to IPCC SSP1-1.9 / NGFS Net Zero 2050 / IEA NZE), Too Little Too Late (>2°C, aligned to IPCC SSP2-4.5 / NGFS NDCs / IEA APS), and Hothouse (>3°C, aligned to IPCC SSP5-8.5). Four time horizons were also selected. The scenarios were developed in accordance with the XRB's guidance on sector-level scenario analysis.
answers.evidence: "The work to compile the narratives was commissioned by the NZBA on behalf of its members, and developed by EY. The aim is to develop a common set of narratives to support a better understanding/assessment of climate-related risks and the reporting expectations against the TCFD recommendations and the Standards. The final outputs of that report include: A common set of scenario narratives and horizons to be used in climate-related risk assessment and disclosures... Three scenario narratives and four time horizons were developed to promote alignment of climate-related scenario analysis and risk disclosures across New Zealand's banking sector... The alignment of the scenarios to the chosen scenario dimensions was done in accordance with the XRB's guidance on sector-level scenario analysis (External Reporting Board, 2022)."
answers.notes: The scenarios were co-produced at the industry (NZBA) level with EY, not solely by CCB NZL. CCB NZL used these common narratives as the basis of its own scenario analysis.

answers.question: Baseline scenarios
answers.answer: Three scenario narratives were used as baselines: (1) Orderly 1.5°C — aligned with IPCC SSP1-1.9 and NGFS Net Zero 2050 / IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (NZE); (2) Too Little Too Late >2°C — aligned with IPCC SSP2-4.5 and NGFS Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) / IEA Announced Pledges (APS); (3) Hothouse >3°C — aligned with IPCC SSP5-8.5. These were developed by EY on behalf of the NZBA and used by CCB NZL as the basis of its scenario analysis.
answers.evidence: "Three scenario narratives and four time horizons were developed to promote alignment of climate-related scenario analysis and risk disclosures across New Zealand's banking sector... Scenario dimensions: Orderly 1.5°C — IPCC SSP1-1.9, NGFS Net Zero 2050, IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (NZE); Too Little Too Late >2°C — IPCC SSP2-4.5, NGFS Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC's), IEA Announced Pledges (APS); Hothouse >3°C — IPCC SSP5-8.5."
answers.notes: Physical risk modelling also used RCP 8.5 as the worst-case scenario for flood risk modelling via Moody's RMS.

answers.question: Model used
answers.answer: CCB NZL used the common scenario narratives developed by the NZBA (commissioned from EY), aligned with IPCC SSP scenarios (SSP1-1.9, SSP2-4.5, SSP5-8.5), NGFS and IEA pathways, and NIWA RCP scenarios (RCP2.6, RCP4.5, RCP8.5). For physical risk modelling on its real estate collaterals, it used the Moody's RMS Inland Flood Model.
answers.evidence: "CCB NZL has utilised the common sets of narratives developed alongside its banking peers as the basis of its scenario analysis." and "CCB NZ has partnered with third party vendors, Valocity and Moody's RMS, to obtain better modelling of the flood risk on its real estate collaterals. The Moody's RMS Inland Flood Model is a fully probabilistic flood model built with data obtained from local organisations and institutions..." and scenario dimensions table showing IPCC SSP1-1.9, SSP2-4.5, SSP5-8.5; NGFS Net Zero 2050, NDCs, Current Policies; NIWA RCP2.6, RCP4.5, RCP8.5.
answers.notes: The NZBA scenario narratives were developed by EY. Physical risk modelling used Moody's RMS Inland Flood Model. Scenario dimensions align with IPCC, NGFS, IEA, and NIWA frameworks.

answers.question: Damage from acute physical risk considered
answers.answer: Yes. CCB NZL considers damage from acute physical risks including flood, extreme weather events (e.g., tropical cyclones), and other weather-related losses. A property is considered high risk if the expected mean damage ratio is greater than 20% as modelled in the RMS Moody's dataset. The bank uses flood risk indicators (flood depth, elevation, distance to coast) against 100, 250, and 500-year return event probabilities, and incorporates large weather event scenarios into its ICAAP stress testing.
answers.evidence: "A property is considered high risk if the expected mean damage ratio is greater than 20% as modelled in the RMS Moody's dataset." and "The Bank incorporated a large weather event scenario into its 2023 ICAAP to assess the quantum of the flow-on impacts, and the Bank's ability to weather such an event." and "damage from heavy precipitation or river flooding represented 60 percent of weather related losses."
answers.notes: The document explicitly uses an Expected Mean Damage Ratio (0–10% = Low Risk, 10–20% = Medium Risk, 20–100% = High Risk) to quantify damage from acute physical risks such as flooding. Acute physical risks are also identified in the scenario framework as "event driven, incl. increase in extreme weather events."

answers.question: Scale of scenarios
answers.answer: The scenarios were developed at the sector level (banking sector), covering both credit-level risks (for priority sectors: Agriculture, Transport, Energy, Manufacturing, and Construction & Property) and organisational-level risks. Three scenario narratives and four time horizons were developed to promote alignment across New Zealand's banking sector, commissioned by the NZBA and developed by EY.
answers.evidence: "Three scenario narratives and four time horizons were developed to promote alignment of climate-related scenario analysis and risk disclosures across New Zealand's banking sector." and "Credit level – Climate-related risks faced by the 'priority' sectors in banks' lending portfolios... Priority sectors were chosen to focus credit level risks on the most material industries to the banking sector. Chosen priority industries are Agriculture, Transport, Energy, Manufacturing, and Construction & Property. Organisational level – Climate-related risks faced by the banks' operations..."
answers.notes: The scenarios were applied at the sector/banking-sector level, with both credit-level and organisational-level risk analysis. The work was commissioned by the NZBA on behalf of its members and developed by EY.

answers.question: Time frames
answers.answer: Four time horizons are used: Immediate term (3 years, year 2025), Short term (10 years, year 2030), Medium term (30 years, year 2050), and Long term (50+ years, year 2080+).
answers.evidence:
Immediate term | Short term | Medium term | Long term
Time horizon: 3 years | 10 years | 30 years | 50+ years
Year relative to 2022: 2025 | 2030 | 2050 | 2080+
Rationale for selection:
- Aligned with stress-testing time horizons / Aligned with average mortgage re-pricing time horizons / Provides a current state assessment
- Aligned with interim emissions reduction targets / Broadly aligned with average maturity profile of business loans
- Aligned with international emissions reduction targets / Aligned with international banking sector climate scenario guidance documents
- Aligned with further materialisation of physical risks, especially important to agriculture, property and segments of the energy sector due to the reliance on hydropower

answers.question: Justification for scenario/model choice
answers.answer: CCB NZL used the common NZBA scenario narratives (developed by EY on behalf of NZBA members) to improve comparability and consistency of climate-related risk disclosures across New Zealand's banking sector. The three scenarios (Orderly 1.5°C, Too Little Too Late >2°C, Hothouse >3°C) were aligned with XRB's guidance on sector-level scenario analysis. Scenario dimensions were mapped to established international frameworks (IPCC SSPs, NGFS, IEA pathways, NIWA RCPs, and CCC pathways). Time horizons were chosen based on alignment with stress-testing horizons, average mortgage re-pricing horizons, interim and international emissions reduction targets, and further materialisation of physical risks. For physical risk modelling, RCP8.5 (worst-case scenario) was used via Moody's RMS Inland Flood Model, a fully probabilistic model built with data from NIWA, LINZ, local regional councils, and ICNZ, based on 50,000 years of continuous simulation.
answers.evidence:
"The work to compile the narratives was commissioned by the NZBA on behalf of its members, and developed by EY. The aim is to develop a common set of narratives to support a better understanding/assessment of climate-related risks and the reporting expectations against the TCFD recommendations and the Standards... These three elements are designed to improve the comparability and consistency of climate-related risk disclosures in the banking sector... The alignment of the scenarios to the chosen scenario dimensions was done in accordance with the XRB's guidance on sector-level scenario analysis (External Reporting Board, 2022)."

"The Moody's RMS Inland Flood Model is a fully probabilistic flood model built with data obtained from local organisations and institutions, including the National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research (NIWA), Land Information New Zealand (LINZ), local regional councils and ICNZ. The model is based on 50,000 years of continuous simulation of the entire precipitation cycle capturing the spatial and temporal correlations of flood risk, and all sources of flood (pluvial and fluvial), resulting in a catalog of 350,000 simulated events."
answers.location_hint: Section 03 Strategy, p.13–14; Appendix A1, p.34
answers.notes: The justification covers both the narrative scenario choice (NZBA/EY framework aligned with XRB guidance and international benchmarks) and the physical risk model choice (Moody's RMS, probabilistic, data-rich). Time horizon rationale is explicitly stated in Table 2.

answers.question: Historic climate impacts
answers.answer: The document references historic climate impacts including: flood accounting for more than 50% of all loss events since 1968, with damage from heavy precipitation or river flooding representing 60% of weather-related losses in New Zealand. Prominent examples of extreme weather events cited are Tropical Cyclone Debbie in 2017 and Tropical Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023. The Bank also incorporated a large weather event scenario into its 2023 ICAAP in response to the increasing number of extreme weather events experienced in New Zealand at the start of 2023.
answers.evidence: "Flood is the second highest insured loss in New Zealand, and the Insurance Council of New Zealand (ICNZ) data shows that since 1968 flood accounted for more than 50 percent of all loss events, and damage from heavy precipitation or river flooding represented 60 percent of weather related losses. In the North Island (where CCB NZL's exposures are predominantly located), flooding is often triggered by heavy rainfall brought by transitioned tropical cyclones. Prominent examples are Tropical Cyclone Debbie in 2017 and Tropical Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023."
answers.notes: The document also notes that "With the increasing number of extreme weather events (as experienced in New Zealand at the start of 2023), the Bank has started incorporating these more acute climate risk factors into its risk modelling" and incorporated a large weather event scenario into its 2023 ICAAP.

answers.question: Direct and indirect physical climate risks
answers.answer: CCB NZL identifies both acute and chronic physical climate risks. Acute risks include increased frequency and severity of extreme weather events (e.g., drought, flood, heatwave, storm surges, sea level rise, precipitation change, temperature change). Chronic risks refer to longer-term shifts in climate patterns. These physical risks manifest at two levels: (1) Credit level – affecting borrowers in priority sectors (Agriculture, Transport, Energy, Manufacturing, Construction & Property), potentially resulting in inability to repay loans, damaged assets/collateral, and increased insurance premiums; and (2) Organisational level – causing damage to the bank's branches, data centres and operations. Physical risk modelling (using RMS Moody's data under RCP 8.5) showed that 0.6% of residential properties and 0.2% of non-residential properties are currently at high risk, rising to 0.7% and 0.5% respectively by 2080.
answers.evidence: "Physical risks are manifested through the increased frequency and severity of acute weather events, or longer-term chronic shifts in climate patterns." / "Physical risks: Acute: Event driven, incl. increase in extreme weather events; Chronic: Longer-term shifts in climate patterns." / "Physical operational risks are those where the impact of climate change causes damage to the banks' branches, data centres and operations." / "Our analysis showed that 0.6% of residential properties, and 0.2% of non-residential properties may be at high risk currently. This increases to 0.7% and 0.5% by 2080, under the worst-case scenario of RCP8.5."
answers.notes: The document covers both direct (organisational/operational) and indirect (credit/lending portfolio) physical climate risks across multiple sectors. Sector-specific physical risks include drought, extreme weather/flood, heatwave, precipitation change, temperature change, and sea level rise.
